raw_case_text:
A 29-year-old woman from Kumba, Cameroon, was admitted in January 2004 to St. John's Hospital and Maternity, Kumba, with a five-day history of fever, emesis, poorly localized abdominal discomfort, myalgias and hepatosplenomegaly. Her total leukocyte count was 1.7 x 109/l, (neutrophils 51%, lymphocytes 43%, monocytes 5%). Urinalysis was normal and thin and thick film examinations of the peripheral blood were negative for malaria. The patient also tested negative for HIV. A blood Widal test however, showed a titre of 80 against "O" (somatic) antigen and 160 against the "H" (flagella) antigen of Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi (recommended cut-off titre in our hospital: >= 1:80 and >= 1:160 for the "O" and "H" antigens respectively). Blood culture grew Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi. Two months prior to her illness, she had suffered from an attack of suspected typhoid fever and had been treated with chloramphenicol 500 mg every 6 hours for 14 days.
Antibiogram of the isolated S. enterica serovar Typhi was performed by disc diffusion techniques as recommended by NCCLS guidelines, Minimum inhibitory concentrations (MIC) of nalidixic acid and ciprofloxacin were determined by agar dilution method. The antibiotic discs used included ampicillin 10 mug (Beecham), co-trimoxazole 1.25/23.75 mug (Roche), chloramphenicol 30 mug (Antibioticos SA), ciprofloxacin 5 mug (Bayer), nalidixic acid 30 mug (Sigma) and ceftriaxone 30 mug (Roche). The isolate was found resistant to nalidixic acid, ampicillin, co-trimoxazole and chloramphenicol, but susceptible to ceftriaxone and ciprofloxacin by disc diffusion test. The MICs of ciprofloxacin and nalidixic acid were 0.5 mug/ml and 32.0 mug/ml respectively. The patient remained febrile after 7 days of oral administration of 500 mg ciprofloxacin every 12 hours. Thereafter, the patient was administered 1 g ceftriaxone every 12 hours intravenously, which rendered her afebrile within four days. Treatment was continued for another 3 days. The patient did not relapse on follow-up.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 29-year-old woman presenting with a 5-day history of fever, emesis, and poorly localized abdominal discomfort.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed acute fever five days prior to admission in January 2004, accompanied by recurrent emesis, poorly localized diffuse abdominal discomfort, and generalized myalgias. Her symptoms progressively worsened over the five-day period prompting hospital admission.
subjective.past_medical_history: Two months prior to current presentation, she experienced an attack of suspected typhoid fever treated with oral chloramphenicol 500 mg every 6 hours for 14 days. She resides in Kumba, Cameroon.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports generalized myalgias and gastrointestinal distress (emesis, abdominal discomfort). No other constitutional complaints detailed.

objective.physical_examination: Abdominal examination revealed palpable hepatosplenomegaly and diffuse abdominal discomfort. Patient was clinically febrile upon admission.
objective.routine_investigations: Total leukocyte count markedly decreased at 1.7 x 10^9/L (neutrophils 51%, lymphocytes 43%, monocytes 5%, demonstrating leukopenia). Urinalysis was normal. Peripheral blood thin and thick smears were negative for Plasmodium falciparum (malaria). HIV rapid screening was negative. Blood Widal serology showed a diagnostic titre of 1:80 against Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi 'O' somatic antigen and 1:160 against 'H' flagella antigen (meeting hospital cut-off criteria).
objective.advanced_workup: Antibiogram via NCCLS disc diffusion demonstrated multidrug resistance to nalidixic acid, ampicillin, co-trimoxazole, and chloramphenicol, with apparent disc susceptibility to ciprofloxacin and ceftriaxone. Agar dilution MIC testing revealed nalidixic acid MIC of 32.0 mcg/mL (resistant) and ciprofloxacin MIC of 0.5 mcg/mL (reduced susceptibility).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Confirmed Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi bacteremia (typhoid fever) based on blood culture growth, presenting as nalidixic acid-resistant S. enterica serovar Typhi (NARST) with reduced ciprofloxacin susceptibility. Differential diagnoses of malaria and HIV were definitively ruled out.
Plan & Outcome: Initially treated with oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg every 12 hours; patient experienced clinical treatment failure, remaining febrile after 7 days. Regimen was switched to intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g every 12 hours, achieving defervescence within four days. Ceftriaxone was continued for a total of 7 days, resulting in complete clinical recovery with no relapse on follow-up.
